claim: Veins in vascular networks continuously reorganize, grow or shrink, to minimize energy dissipation.
source: Veins in vascular networks, such as in blood vasculature or leaf networks, continuously reorganize, grow or shrink, to minimize energy dissipation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of vascular networks.

claim: Flow shear stress on vein walls has been set forth as the local driver for a vein's continuous adaptation.
source: Flow shear stress on vein walls has been set forth as the local driver for a vein's continuous adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a previously proposed mechanism.

claim: Shear feedback alone cannot account for the observed diversity of vein dynamics.
source: Yet, shear feedback alone cannot account for the observed diversity of vein dynamics – a puzzle made harder by scarce spatiotemporal data.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key problem addressed by the study.

claim: Shear rate feeds back on vein radius with a time delay of 1–3 min.
source: Quantitative analysis of our data reveals that (a) shear rate indeed feeds back on vein radius, yet, with a time delay of 1–3 min.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Vein fate is determined by parameters that integrate the entire network's architecture.
source: The model reveals that (b) vein fate is determined by parameters – local pressure or relative vein resistance – which integrate the entire network's architecture, as they result from global conservation of fluid volume.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding from the model.

claim: Avalanches of network reorganization events cause entire clusters of veins to vanish.
source: Finally, we observe avalanches of network reorganization events that cause entire clusters of veins to vanish.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations in Figure 6.

claim: The findings are expected to play a role across flow-based vascular networks.
source: As the network architecture integrating parameters intrinsically arise from laminar fluid flow in veins, we expect our findings to play a role across flow-based vascular networks.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Continuous reorganization is integral to a network's success.
source: Continuous reorganization is integral to a network's success: veins perpetually grow and shrink (Lucitti et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2012; Hu and Cai, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Reorganization patterns at the network scale remain a puzzle.
source: While vein dynamics are usually observed for individual veins (Kurz, 2000), reorganization patterns at the network scale remain a puzzle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Understanding network reorganization is crucial to shed light on the mechanics of development and widespread diseases.
source: Yet, understanding network reorganization is crucial to shed light on the mechanics of development (Chen et al., 2012) and widespread diseases (Meyer et al., 2008; Pries et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The physics that governs pervading and laminar fluid flows is the same across diverse vasculature systems.
source: While the biological makeup of vasculature systems is quite diverse, the physics that governs pervading and laminar fluid flows is the same (Alim, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Murray introduced the idea that shear stress exerted by fluid flows on a vein wall determines vein radius size almost a century ago.
source: Already almost a century ago, Murray introduced the idea that shear stress exerted by fluid flows on a vein wall determines vein radius size (Murray, 1926).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Murray's work.

claim: At steady state, veins minimize viscous dissipation while constrained by a constant metabolic cost to sustain the vein.
source: Within his framework, at steady state, veins minimize viscous dissipation while constrained by a constant metabolic cost to sustain the vein.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of Murray's framework.

claim: Solving the minimization problem yields that shear stress should be constant among veins.
source: Solving the minimization problem yields that shear stress, driver of viscous dissipation, should be constant among veins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of Murray's framework.

claim: Data on optimal static network morphologies agrees very well with Murray's predictions across very different forms of life.
source: Data on optimal static network morphologies agrees very well with Murray's predictions, strikingly across very different forms of life; from animals (West et al., 1997; Kassab, 2006), to plants (West et al., 1997; McCulloh et al., 2003) and slime molds (Akita et al., 2017; Fricker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Fluid flow physics is key to understanding vascular morphologies.
source: Fluid flow physics is, therefore, key to understanding vascular morphologies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the agreement with Murray's predictions.

claim: Data on vein dynamics during spontaneous reorganization is limited due to the difficulty of acquiring time-resolved data covering entire networks.
source: Data on vein dynamics (Chen et al., 2012; Baumgarten and Hauser, 2013; Rosenfeld et al., 2016; Chang and Roper, 2019; Sugden et al., 2017), even during spontaneous reorganization, is limited due to the difficulty of acquiring time-resolved data covering entire networks.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Observation of network excerpts suggests that flow shear stress alone can not account for the diversity of observed dynamics.
source: Observation of network excerpts suggests that flow shear stress alone can not account for the diversity of observed dynamics (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A number of vein adaptation models have been introduced.
source: In light of scarce experimental observations, a number of vein adaptation models have been introduced (Hacking et al., 1996; Taber, 1998b; Taber, 1998a; Zhou et al., 1999; Pries et al., 2005; Baumgarten and Hauser, 2013; Hu and Cai, 2013; Secomb et al., 2013; Akita et al., 2017; Katifori et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The mechanisms that govern vein adaptation and thereby network reorganization can only be conclusively determined experimentally.
source: Yet, the mechanisms that govern vein adaptation and thereby network reorganization can only be conclusively determined experimentally.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a motivation for the experimental approach.

claim: P. polycephalum's body is reduced to approximately two dimensions.
source: Since the organisms' body is reduced to approximately two dimensions (Baumgarten and Hauser, 2013; Alim et al., 2013; Fricker et al., 2017), it opens up the unique possibility to quantify vein dynamics and fluid flows simultaneously in the entire network.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: P. polycephalum opens up the unique possibility to quantify vein dynamics and fluid flows simultaneously in the entire network.
source: Since the organisms' body is reduced to approximately two dimensions (Baumgarten and Hauser, 2013; Alim et al., 2013; Fricker et al., 2017), it opens up the unique possibility to quantify vein dynamics and fluid flows simultaneously in the entire network.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key advantage of the experimental system.

claim: Flows in the veins arise from rhythmic contractions of vein walls due to actomyosin activity in the vein cortex.
source: Flows in the veins arise from rhythmic contractions of vein walls due to actomyosin activity in the vein cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of P. polycephalum.

claim: The flows oscillatory component changes rapidly on 1 min to 2 min.
source: As the flows oscillatory component changes rapidly on 1 min to 2 min (Stewart and Stewart, 1959; Isenberg and Wohlfarth-Bottermann, 1976), average flows dominate long-term vein adaptation dynamics on 10 min and more.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Average flows dominate long-term vein adaptation dynamics on 10 min and more.
source: As the flows oscillatory component changes rapidly on 1 min to 2 min (Stewart and Stewart, 1959; Isenberg and Wohlfarth-Bottermann, 1976), average flows dominate long-term vein adaptation dynamics on 10 min and more.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of the oscillatory component.

claim: Vein dynamics in P. polycephalum are observed using two complementary imaging techniques: close-up observation of single veins or full network imaging.
source: We observe vein dynamics in P. polycephalum specimen using two complementary imaging techniques, either close-up observation of single veins or full network imaging (Figure 1 and additional methods in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Diverse, complex, yet reproducible trajectories are found when relating time-averaged shear rate to time-averaged vein radius.
source: We relate time-averaged shear rate to time-averaged vein radius and find diverse, complex, yet reproducible trajectories (Figure 1A, B.iv, see also Appendix 1—figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 5 for additional datasets).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1A, B.iv.

claim: Out of 200 randomly chosen veins in the full network, 80 are shrinking veins, 100 are stable veins, and 20 are not classifiable.
source: To illustrate this diversity, out of 200 randomly chosen veins in the full network of Figure 1B, we find 80 shrinking veins, 100 stable veins, and 20 are not classifiable.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantification of vein diversity.

claim: In shrinking veins, the relation between shear rate and vein adaption is particularly ambiguous.
source: In shrinking veins, the relation between shear rate and vein adaption is particularly ambiguous.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a key observation.

claim: As the radius of a vein shrinks, the shear rate either monotonically decreases, or monotonically increases, or increases at first and decreases again.
source: As the radius of a vein shrinks, the shear rate either monotonically decreases (pink b in Figure 1B.iv), or, monotonically increases (pink d), or, increases at first and decreases again (pink c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.iv.

claim: For the specimen of Figure 1B, out of the 80 shrinking veins, monotonic decrease is observed for 25%, monotonic increase for 40%, and non-monotonic trajectories 15% of the time.
source: For the specimen of Figure 1B, out of the 80 shrinking veins, monotonic decrease is observed for 25%, monotonic increase for 40%, and non-monotonic trajectories 15% of the time.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantification of shrinking vein dynamics.

claim: The remaining 20% of vanishing veins are unclassifiable, as their recorded trajectories are too short to allow for any classification.
source: The remaining 20% of vanishing veins are unclassifiable, as their recorded trajectories are too short to allow for any classification.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation for unclassifiable veins.

claim: Out of the 12 close-up veins investigated, 4 shrink and vanish, either with monotonic or non-monotonic dynamics.
source: Out of the 12 close-up veins investigated, 4 shrink and vanish, either with monotonic or non-monotonic dynamics (see also Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantification of close-up vein dynamics.

claim: Stable veins usually perform looping trajectories in the shear rate-radius space.
source: In contrast, stable veins have a specific shear rate-radius relation: usually, stable veins perform looping trajectories in the shear rate-radius space (blue arrows in Figure 1A, B.iv).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1A, B.iv.

claim: In the full network, these loops circle clockwise for 80% of 100 observed stable veins.
source: In the full network, these loops circle clockwise for 80% of 100 observed stable veins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantification of stable vein dynamics.

claim: Out of the 12 close-up veins investigated, 6 veins show stable clockwise feedback, 1 shows stable anticlockwise feedback, and 1 is not classifiable.
source: Out of the 12 close-up veins investigated, 6 veins show stable clockwise feedback, 1 shows stable anticlockwise feedback, and 1 is not classifiable.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantification of close-up vein dynamics.

claim: Clockwise circling corresponds to an in/decrease in shear rate followed by an in/decrease in vein radius, thus, hinting at a shear rate feedback on local vein adaptation.
source: Clockwise circling corresponds to an in/decrease in shear rate followed by an in/decrease in vein radius, thus, hinting at a shear rate feedback on local vein adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the clockwise circling.

claim: The circular shape of stable vein trajectories suggests that there is a time delay between changes in shear rate and subsequent vein radius changes.
source: In addition, the circular shape of stable vein trajectories suggests that there is a time delay between changes in shear rate and subsequent vein radius changes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the circular trajectories.

claim: Despite displaying comparable shear rate and vein radii at the beginning of data acquisition, some veins are stable while others vanish.
source: First, despite displaying comparable shear rate and vein radii at the beginning of our data acquisition, some veins are stable (blue a in Figure 1A, B.iv), while others vanish (pink b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1A, B.iv.

claim: Dangling ends have low shear rate, due to flow arresting at the very end of the vein.
source: We observe that dangling ends have low shear rate, due to flow arresting at the very end of the vein (dark purple terminal veins).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: Some dangling ends will grow despite having low shear rate.
source: Yet, some dangling ends will grow (i.e red dot in Figure 1B.i), in contradiction again with the assumption that 'low shear results in a shrinking vein'.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.i.

claim: Small veins located in the middle of the organism show high shear rate, yet, will vanish.
source: Finally, small veins located in the middle of the organism show high shear rate, yet, will vanish (yellow arrow in Figure 1B.ii, other examples in Appendix 1—figure 4C and Appendix 1—figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: The hypothesis that veins with low shear rate should vanish cannot be reconciled with the data.
source: Therefore, the hypothesis that veins with low shear rate should vanish, as they cannot sustain the mechanical effort (Koller et al., 1993; Hoefer et al., 2013), cannot be reconciled with our data.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Geometrical vein characteristics are directly related to vein radius, thus in contradiction with the observation that veins with similar radius can experience different fates.
source: In fact, geometrical vein characteristics are directly related to vein radius, thus in contradiction with our observation that veins with similar radius can experience different fates (stable blue a in Figure 1iv and vanishing pink b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation for why geometrical characteristics don't determine fate.

claim: Additional feedback parameters must play a role in determining vein fate.
source: Therefore, additional feedback parameters must play a role.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Within the force balance derivation, the cross-linked actin fiber cortex composing the vein wall responds with a force in the normal direction compared to tangential shear and drives veins to dilate or shrink in response to shear.
source: Within the force balance derivation, the cross-linked actin fiber cortex composing the vein wall responds with a force in the normal direction compared to tangential shear and, hence, drives veins to dilate or shrink in response to shear (Gardel et al., 2008; Janmey et al., 2007; see Appendix 2.1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Experimental data measuring the anisotropic response of fibers suggest a quadratic dependence of the change in fibers thickness on the applied shear.
source: Experimental data measuring this anisotropic response of fibers in Janmey et al., 2007; Vahabi et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2009 suggest a quadratic dependence of the change in fibers thickness on the applied shear.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The quadratic dependence is consistent with the top-down phenomenological result of Hu et al., 2012.
source: This quadratic dependence is also consistent with the top-down phenomenological result of Hu et al., 2012.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Lag times between peaks in time-averaged shear rate and radius dynamics range from 1 min to 10 min.
source: Figure 1iii indeed shows lag times between peaks in time-averaged shear rate and radius dynamics, ranging from 1 min to 10 min.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1iii.

claim: Time delays are recorded if the maximum is significant only, with a threshold of 0.5.
source: Time delays are recorded if the maximum is significant only, that is if the cross-correlation is high enough, and here we choose the threshold to be 0.5.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a method for selecting significant time delays.

claim: Slight changes in the threshold do not affect the results significantly.
source: Note, that slight changes in the threshold do not affect our results significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a robustness check.

claim: Both positive and negative time delays are recorded.
source: Both positive and negative time delays are recorded.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a characteristic of the analysis.

claim: 15 times more veins with positive time delays than with negative time delays are found for the specimen of Figure 1B.
source: Overall, we find 15 times more veins with positive time delays than with negative time delays for the specimen of Figure 1B (full time delay distribution in Appendix 2—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Positive time delays clearly establish a causality link between shear rate magnitude and radius adaptation.
source: This clearly establishes a causality link between shear rate magnitude and radius adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the positive time delays.

claim: Similar results are found when repeating the analysis over different full network specimens and close-up veins.
source: We repeat the analysis over different full network specimens (Appendix 2—figure 2) and close-up veins (Appendix 2—figure 3) and find similar results.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a validation of the findings.

claim: The similarity between t_delay and T is not an artifact of the analysis.
source: This is not an artifact of the analysis (see benchmark test in Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a clarification.

claim: The similarity between t_delay and T hints that the cross-linked actomyosin and contractile cortex are key players in the delay.
source: Rather, it hints that the cross-linked actomyosin and contractile cortex are key players in the delay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation.

claim: Measured data on the contractile response of cross-linked fibers exhibits a time delay of about 1–30 s for in vitro gels.
source: Measured data on the contractile response of cross-linked fibers (Gardel et al., 2008; Janmey et al., 2007; Vahabi et al., 2018) exhibits a time delay of about 1–30 s for in vitro gels.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The turnover time for actin filaments in living cells ranges from 10 s to 30 s.
source: For example, the turnover time for actin filaments in living cells ranges from 10 s to 30 s (Fritzsche et al., 2013; Livne et al., 2014; Colombelli et al., 2009), while the viscoelastic relaxation time is 100 s (Joanny and Prost, 2009), both timescales close to our measured time delay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The viscoelastic relaxation time is 100 s.
source: For example, the turnover time for actin filaments in living cells ranges from 10 s to 30 s (Fritzsche et al., 2013; Livne et al., 2014; Colombelli et al., 2009), while the viscoelastic relaxation time is 100 s (Joanny and Prost, 2009), both timescales close to our measured time delay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The model with the adaptation rule Equation 1 and the time delay shear rate sensing Equation 2 quantitatively accounts for the observed dynamics with physiologically relevant parameters.
source: We further verify that our model with the adaptation rule Equation 1 and the time delay shear rate sensing Equation 2 quantitatively accounts for the observed dynamics with physiologically relevant parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a validation of the model.

claim: 12 close-up data sets and 15 randomly chosen veins of the full network in Figure 1B are fitted.
source: We fit our 12 close-up data sets, as well as 15 randomly chosen veins of the full network in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a description of the fitting procedure.

claim: A remarkable agreement between fit and data is found.
source: Overall, we find a remarkable agreement between fit and data (see example in Figure 2D and Appendix 2 for more results).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: The minimal ingredients of the model are sufficient to reproduce experimental data.
source: This suggests that the minimal ingredients of this model are sufficient to reproduce experimental data.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the fit quality.

claim: Fitting parameters resulted in physically reasonable values in all samples.
source: In all samples, fitting parameters resulted in physically reasonable values.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a validation of the model.

claim: Significant adaptation is observed over the timescale of 10–100 min.
source: This 10–100 min is indeed the timescale over which we observe significant adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a validation of the fit result.

claim: Reorganization of biological matter occurs on similar timescales in other comparable systems, from 15 min for individual cells to several days for blood vasculature.
source: Reorganization of biological matter occurs on similar timescales in other comparable systems, from 15 min for individual cells to several days for blood vasculature (Livne et al., 2014; Landau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The model yields better results if the data is fitted over intermediate time frames (15 min to 40 min), exceeding results of fitting over longer time frames (40 min to 100 min).
source: Finally, we find that our model yields better results if we fit the data over intermediate time frames (15 min to 40 min), exceeding results of fitting over longer time frames (40 min to 100 min).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation about the fitting procedure.

claim: The origin of different vein fates resides in the evolution of the rest of the network.
source: We will show that the origin of different fates resides in the evolution of the rest of the network.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a preview of the upcoming analysis.

claim: Such a reduction of a flow network to a simple equivalent flow circuit is always possible due to Norton's theorem.
source: Such a reduction of a flow network to a simple equivalent flow circuit is always possible due to Norton's theorem (Morris, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The set of fixed points was also found in a related theoretical study that investigates a phenomenological model resembling Equation 1, yet without any time delay.
source: The set of fixed points was also found in a related theoretical study that investigates a phenomenological model resembling Equation 1, yet without any time delay, and examining the stability of a vein, or resistance, connected to a pressure source and another resistance (Hacking et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The presence of the three fixed points is universal.
source: This suggests that the presence of the three fixed points is universal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the comparison with previous work.

claim: The active stress sustains the contractile activity of the vein, and is an indirect measure of the metabolic or energetic consumption in the vein.
source: The active stress sustains the contractile activity of the vein, and is, therefore, an indirect measure of the metabolic or energetic consumption in the vein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the active stress.

claim: According to shear rate measures, the shear rate is large in a shrinking vein, preconditioning the vein to grow according to previous works.
source: However, according to shear rate measures (see yellow arrow in Figure 1B.ii), the shear rate is large in that vein, preconditioning the vein to grow, according to previous works (Taber, 1998a; Hacking et al., 1996; Hu et al., 2012; Secomb et al., 2013; Pries et al., 1998; Pries et al., 2005; Hu and Cai, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: Dangling ends either vanish or grow but never show stably oscillating trajectories.
source: As observed in our data, dangling ends are typical examples of veins that can start with very similar shear rate and radius and yet suffer radically different fates (Figure 1B.i, ii, Figure 5A). Dangling ends either vanish or grow but never show stably oscillating trajectories.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figures 1B and 5A.

claim: Dangling ends are only connected to the rest of the network by a single node.
source: Topologically, and unlike the middle vein considered in Figure 3A, dangling ends are only connected to the rest of the network by a single node.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Dangling veins can only shrink or grow.
source: Using this expression instead of Equation 3 and analyzing the dynamical system with Equations 1; 2, we find that dangling veins can only shrink or grow (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the dynamic system analysis.

claim: When a vein is connected to a large input pressure, one expects the vein to open up.
source: This agrees with physical intuition: when a vein is connected to a large input pressure, one expects the vein to open up.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the observation.

claim: The shear rate threshold to grow is lowered by the high local pressure in dangling ends.
source: Notice, however, that here the mechanism is subtle. The shear rate itself is not large. Rather, the shear rate threshold to grow is lowered by the high local pressure.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a clarification of the mechanism.

claim: Local pressure is connected to dangling end fate and is a prime example of the importance of integrating network architecture.
source: Local pressure is thus connected to dangling end fate: it is a prime example of the importance of integrating network architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Initially very similar and spatially close parallel veins may suffer opposite fates.
source: Parallel veins are another example in which initially very similar and spatially close veins may suffer opposite fates; see Figure 5B.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Often, both parallel veins will eventually vanish, yet what determines which vanishes first is a question.
source: Often, both parallel veins will eventually vanish, yet what determines which vanishes first?
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a question to be addressed.

claim: Loopy structures are often observed in P. polycephalum.
source: Finally, loopy structures i.e. a long vein connected at both ends to the remaining network, are often observed in P. polycephalum.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation.

claim: Loops start shrinking in their very middle despite the almost homogeneous vein diameter and shear rate along the entire loop.
source: Surprisingly, we experimentally observe loops to start shrinking in their very middle (Figure 5C, Appendix 1—figure 4F and Appendix 1—figure 5F) despite the almost homogeneous vein diameter and shear rate along the entire loop.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The phenomenon of loops shrinking in the middle resides in the network architecture.
source: This phenomenon again resides in the network architecture, and we can rationalize it with an equivalent flow circuit (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation.

claim: When a vein segment in the loop shrinks, mass has to be redistributed to the rest of the network, increasing shear rate in the outer segments and preventing their disappearance.
source: When a vein segment in the loop shrinks, mass has to be redistributed to the rest of the network. This increases shear rate in the outer segments, preventing the disappearance of the outer segments of the loop.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation.

claim: Once the center segment has disappeared, both outer segments follow the dynamics of dangling ends.
source: Once the center segment has disappeared, both outer segments follow the dynamics of dangling ends.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the center segment disappearing.

claim: As soon as a vein disappears, the network's architecture changes: flows must redistribute, and vein connections are updated.
source: Importantly, we find that as soon as a vein disappears, the network's architecture changes: flows must redistribute, and vein connections are updated.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation.

claim: An initially stable vein may become unstable as the network architecture changes.
source: Hence, an initially stable vein may become unstable.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the network architecture changing.

claim: Vein fates dramatically evolve over time.
source: Vein fates, thus, dramatically evolve over time.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Veins vanish sequentially in time in a disappearing network region.
source: Observing a disappearing network region over time, we find that veins vanish sequentially in time (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6A, B.

claim: The few veins with high relative resistance vanish first.
source: As expected, the few veins with high relative resistance (red arrows in Figure 6A, 2 min) indeed vanish first (black crosses in Figure 6A, 5 min).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Veins that were stable before are now predicted to be unstable.
source: Veins that were stable before are now predicted to be unstable.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the architecture change.

claim: This avalanche-like pattern, in which individual vanishing veins cause neighboring veins to become unstable, repeats itself until the entire region disappears in less than 15 min.
source: This avalanche-like pattern, in which individual vanishing veins cause neighboring veins to become unstable, repeats itself until the entire region disappears in less than 15 min (Appendix 1—figure 4F and Appendix 1—figure 5F show similar avalanches in other specimens).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation.

claim: A vanishing vein may rarely also stabilize a previously unstable vein.
source: Note that a vanishing vein may rarely also stabilize a previously unstable vein (Figure 6A, 16 min, blue arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The fundamental origin of avalanches of vanishing veins can be narrowed down to network architecture.
source: The fundamental origin of these avalanches of vanishing veins can be narrowed down again to network architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion.

claim: A model network region is explored, inspired by a region in an actual specimen.
source: We explore a model network region, inspired by a region in an actual specimen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: The perturbed vein's relative resistance may become greater than 1, making the vein unstable.
source: The perturbed vein's relative resistance thus may become greater than 1, making the vein unstable.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the perturbation.

claim: As the vein vanishes, two network nodes are removed, and individual veins previously connected through the node now become a single longer vein.
source: As the vein vanishes, two network nodes are removed, and individual veins previously connected through the node now become a single longer vein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the vein vanishing.

claim: A longer vein has a higher hydraulic resistance.
source: A longer vein has a higher hydraulic resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a consequence of the vein becoming longer.

claim: The 'new' longer vein also becomes unstable.
source: Hence, the 'new' longer vein also becomes unstable (blue in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Once the longer vein vanishes, another neighboring vein becomes longer and unstable.
source: Once it vanishes, in turn, another neighboring vein becomes longer and unstable (green in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: In the simple mechanistic model, the series of events follows an avalanche principle similar to that observed in experiments.
source: In our simple mechanistic model, the series of events follows an avalanche principle similar to that observed in our experiments: a vanishing vein disturbs local architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a comparison between the model and experiments.

claim: A vanishing vein disturbs local architecture, modifying the relative resistance of nearby veins and hence their stability.
source: In our simple mechanistic model, the series of events follows an avalanche principle similar to that observed in our experiments: a vanishing vein disturbs local architecture. This modifies the relative resistance of nearby veins and hence their stability.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation of the avalanche principle.
